strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful problem: unsupervised, instance-specific discovery of symmetry distributions, including the important nuisance that class-pose methods produce arbitrary canonical orientations.

The proposed canonical orientation normalization is simple, interpretable, and technically well motivated: using the empirical Fréchet mean to remove the arbitrary pose offset is a natural and useful idea.

The paper provides a clear connection to class-pose decomposition methods and includes a theoretical proposition explaining when the normalized relative-pose distribution recovers the intended identity-centered distribution.
Experiments span both SO(2) image settings and SO(3) molecular conformations, which is broader than many prior symmetry-learning evaluations.
The qualitative results on canonicalization and the OOD pose detection application help communicate why normalized, comparable symmetry distributions are useful.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental: the core method is essentially a post-hoc centering of pose samples from an existing class-pose decomposition model, and the paper does not fully establish that this is a substantial algorithmic advance over natural baselines using circular/Riemannian means.

The empirical evaluation lacks strong quantitative comparisons to relevant baselines. SGM and IE-AE are mostly discussed qualitatively, while methods for learned/partial equivariance are not compared on comparable metrics for symmetry recovery or OOD detection.

Most ground-truth symmetry distributions are synthetically imposed after dataset preprocessing. The GEOM experiment uses aligned conformers with artificial matrix-Fisher rotations, so the claim of discovering real-world 3D symmetry distributions is stronger than the evidence supports.

The theoretical result relies on strong assumptions: accurate equivariant pose estimation, clean class neighborhoods in invariant space, small residual non-group variation, uniqueness and stability of Fréchet means, and appropriate right-invariant geometry. These assumptions are not empirically stress-tested.

The k-NN approximation to equivalence classes is central but fragile. The paper only gives a limited neighborhood-size study and does not evaluate failure modes under class overlap, multimodal invariant embeddings, poor IE-AE reconstruction, or imbalanced class sampling.

The 3D results are not very rigorously quantified. Reporting that roughly 80% of molecules fall below a visually chosen MSE threshold is weak, and the meaning of matrix-Fisher parameter MSE is not sufficiently calibrated against distributional distances or downstream utility.

Ablations are limited. The paper would benefit from direct comparisons against unnormalized pose distributions, alternative centering rules, different density estimators, different class-pose backbones, and oracle neighborhoods/labels.

The learned inference mappings Θ and Λ are trained from pseudo-labels produced by RECON itself, making it hard to separate the quality of the normalization procedure from the quality and biases of the pseudo-label regression stage.

Some claims are overstated, especially around unsupervised discovery and real-world 3D symmetries, given that the group G is fixed in advance and the evaluated pose distributions are largely controlled augmentations.

strengths: The paper identifies a real limitation of class-pose decomposition methods: learned canonical orientations are arbitrary, making relative pose distributions hard to compare across instances or classes.
The proposed normalization via a group Fréchet mean is simple, geometrically interpretable, and in principle applicable beyond SO(2), including SO(3).
The manuscript is reasonably well organized and includes both image and molecular-graph experiments, with implementation details and hyperparameters in the appendix.
The qualitative visualizations make the intended benefit of identity-centered symmetry distributions easy to understand.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution appears limited: once one has an equivariant pose estimator and a neighborhood/class estimate, recentering the observed group elements by their Fréchet mean is a fairly direct post-processing step. The paper does not convincingly establish that this is a substantial methodological advance over existing class-pose or symmetry-discovery methods.

The evaluation is not competitive for a top-tier AI venue. There are essentially no strong quantitative baselines for symmetry recovery, canonicalization quality, or OOD pose detection. Closely related methods such as SGM, Augerino, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, and weight-sharing symmetry discovery are discussed but not compared in a meaningful experimental table.

The main experimental settings are heavily synthetic or controlled. MNIST/FashionMNIST symmetries are label-dependent artificial rotations, and the GEOM experiment applies artificial matrix-Fisher rotations after alignment. This weakens the claim of discovering real-world unknown symmetries.

The 3D/molecular contribution is overstated. The molecules are pre-aligned, assigned synthetic rotation distributions, and evaluated against those injected distributions. This is useful as a stress test but does not demonstrate discovery of natural molecular symmetry distributions.

The theoretical result relies on strong assumptions that are not validated in practice, including accurate equivariant pose estimation, compactness/continuity, small residual noise, well-behaved Fréchet means, and neighborhoods that approximate true equivalence classes. The proof mostly formalizes that a translated distribution can be recentered if the translation can be estimated.

The practical method depends critically on k-nearest-neighbor neighborhoods in the learned invariant space, but this approximation is fragile and only lightly studied. The MNIST k ablation is insufficient to establish robustness across datasets, class imbalance, overlapping classes, or continuous variation.

The quantitative reporting is weak. Several figures are qualitative or hard to interpret, the GEOM MSE scale is not well motivated, and statements such as roughly 80% of molecules being accurate below MSE < 800 are based on subjective visualization rather than principled thresholds.

The learned mappings Θ and Λ are trained on pseudo-labels generated by the same method, but there is limited analysis of pseudo-label noise, generalization to unseen classes, or failure modes when the IE-AE representation is imperfect.

The OOD pose detection application is underdeveloped: AUCs are reported without baselines, confidence intervals, threshold analysis, or a clear demonstration that RECON is necessary relative to simpler likelihood or pose-estimation alternatives.

Claims about being unsupervised and instance-specific are somewhat weakened by the experimental construction: class-dependent synthetic distributions are used, and the method depends on latent neighborhoods that may implicitly recover dataset labels rather than more general instance-level structure.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and timely problem: discovering instance-specific, approximate symmetry distributions rather than assuming a fixed global equivariance group.

The core idea of correcting arbitrary class-pose canonicals via Fréchet-mean canonical orientation normalization is elegant, interpretable, and well motivated by a real limitation of IE-AE/SGM-style decompositions.

The method is conceptually simple and broadly applicable to any backbone that yields invariant and equivariant pose components, making the contribution more reusable than a single architecture-specific trick.

The paper provides a clear theoretical statement connecting observed relative pose distributions to the intrinsic symmetry distribution under explicit assumptions, and the proof gives useful intuition for why right-translation by the estimated centroid should work.

Experiments span both SO(2) image data and SO(3) molecular conformations, which is a valuable step beyond the common 2D rotation setting. The 3D molecular experiment is ambitious and strengthens the paper's relevance.

The qualitative results are convincing: normalized distributions become identity-centered and comparable, and the canonical reconstructions are visibly more natural than unnormalized IE-AE/SGM canonicals.
The OOD pose detection application is a nice demonstration that the recovered distributions can support downstream use, not just visualization.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is weaker than the scope of the claims. Most ground-truth symmetry distributions are synthetically imposed through rotations, including the GEOM experiment after alignment, so the paper does not fully demonstrate discovery of naturally occurring real-world symmetries.

Quantitative comparisons to strong baselines are limited. The paper discusses SGM, Augerino, Partial G-CNNs, VP G-CNNs, and IE-AE, but does not provide enough head-to-head quantitative evaluation against the most relevant alternatives for symmetry recovery or downstream tasks.

The 3D evaluation relies heavily on matrix-Fisher parameter MSE and visual thresholds such as MSE < 800; it is not obvious how these errors translate into meaningful distributional accuracy on SO(3), and alternative metrics such as likelihood, Wasserstein/geodesic distances, or calibration are not sufficiently explored.

The theoretical result depends on strong assumptions: small non-group residuals, continuity/equivariance of the learned pose map, compactness, uniqueness and stability of Fréchet means, and reliable recovery of equivalence classes via nearest neighbors in invariant space. These assumptions may fail in precisely the ambiguous or multimodal symmetry cases the method targets.

The k-nearest-neighbor approximation to latent equivalence classes is central but only lightly ablated. Sensitivity to latent clustering failures, class imbalance, mixed classes, and high-dimensional neighbor errors remains underexplored.

The method still requires specifying the transformation group G in advance, so it does not solve the broader problem of discovering unknown symmetry groups, despite some wording that may suggest more general symmetry discovery.

For SO(3), the paper appears to estimate the offset using the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution rather than the Fréchet mean used in the theory; the relationship between this practical estimator and the theoretical normalization should be clarified.
Reproducibility is somewhat limited by reliance on hidden code links and expensive training, especially the molecular experiment, though the appendix does provide useful implementation details.

strengths: The paper identifies a meaningful limitation of class-pose decomposition methods: learned canonicals can have arbitrary, class-dependent orientations, making recovered pose distributions hard to compare or use downstream.

The proposed RECON procedure is simple and intuitive: estimate the pose offset of a local invariant-space neighborhood via a Fréchet-type centroid and right-normalize the relative poses. This makes the method architecture-agnostic for any backbone that exposes invariant features and relative pose estimates.
The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, with useful figures that communicate the difference between arbitrary class-pose canonicals and the proposed data-aligned canonicalization.

The empirical scope is broader than many symmetry-discovery papers, covering SO(2) image rotations and a nontrivial SO(3) molecular graph setting, plus downstream demonstrations for OOD pose detection and test-time canonicalization.

The appendices provide a fair amount of implementation detail, including architectures, training schedules, neighborhood size analysis, and additional diagnostics for the invariant-space neighborhood quality.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. The main method is essentially post-hoc centering of relative pose estimates using a Fréchet or robust Fréchet mean over nearest neighbors. This is useful, but the paper does not fully establish it as a major conceptual advance over existing canonicalization, pose-normalization, or symmetry-discovery methods.

The empirical evaluation relies heavily on synthetic, known transformation distributions: rotated MNIST/FashionMNIST and GEOM-QM9 molecules augmented by sampled SO(3) rotations. This validates recovery under controlled assumptions, but gives limited evidence that the method discovers unknown real-world symmetries rather than recovering injected augmentations.

Baselines are too limited for a top-tier claim. The key quantitative comparisons are mostly against IE-AE-style unnormalized relative poses, while closely related methods such as SGM, learned canonicalization/frame averaging approaches, Augerino/partial equivariance methods, and stronger heuristic centering or clustering baselines are not quantitatively compared across the main tasks.

The theory depends on strong assumptions that are not sufficiently stress-tested: accurate equivariant pose estimates, compactness/continuity, well-formed invariant-space equivalence classes, small non-group residuals, unique Fréchet means, and appropriate right-invariant geometry. These assumptions are central to Proposition 3.1 but may fail in realistic data.

There are inconsistencies and underspecified choices around the estimator actually used. The main text motivates Fréchet and Tukey-Fréchet means, while the SO(3) implementation estimates the centering rotation as the mode of a fitted matrix-Fisher distribution; the relationship between this estimator and the theoretical Fréchet normalization is not clearly justified.

The robust Tukey-Fréchet extension is weakly supported. It is motivated with toy SO(2) examples, but there is no substantial ablation showing when it matters, how the cutoff parameter is selected, or whether it improves the reported main results.

The downstream test-time canonicalization experiments are not fully convincing. RECON is trained on the rotated data distribution and then used to help classifiers trained on unrotated data, but comparisons to other practical inference-time alignment methods or augmentation-based baselines are missing, and the IE-AE canonicalization baseline is predictably disadvantaged by arbitrary orientation.

Claims such as 'first demonstrations in 3D' and broad architecture-agnostic group invariance are somewhat overstated given that the 3D evaluation is based on controlled synthetic global rotations of molecular conformers and a specific IE-AE/SEGNN pipeline.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the code is only promised or hidden, and several important details such as hyperparameter search ranges, variance across seeds, confidence intervals, and computational cost tradeoffs are not reported systematically.

The error analysis is shallow. The paper reports aggregate MSE/AUC/accuracy and some visual examples, but gives limited insight into failure modes, sensitivity to neighborhood contamination, class imbalance, multimodal pose distributions, or cases where invariant features do not cluster by true object identity.

strengths: The paper targets a meaningful problem: discovering instance-specific pose/symmetry distributions from unlabeled data and correcting the arbitrary canonical orientations produced by class-pose decomposition models.

The central normalization idea is simple and interpretable: estimate a class-specific pose offset via a Fréchet-style mean and right-multiply relative poses to obtain distributions centered around a natural reference frame.
The paper is reasonably readable and includes useful appendices with implementation details, proofs, and additional analyses such as neighborhood-size sensitivity and kNN hit rates.
The authors attempt to go beyond standard 2D rotation experiments by including an SO(3) molecular setting and by demonstrating downstream uses for OOD pose detection and test-time canonicalization.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited relative to the strength of the claims. The method is essentially a post-hoc centering/calibration step on top of existing class-pose decomposition models, and the paper does not convincingly establish this as a major conceptual advance over existing canonicalization, symmetry-learning, or pose-normalization methods.

The evaluation is heavily synthetic. MNIST/FashionMNIST rotations are manually imposed by class, and the GEOM-QM9 SO(3) symmetries are also artificially assigned using matrix-Fisher rotations. This leaves weak evidence that the method discovers naturally occurring, unknown symmetries in real data.

Baselines are inadequate. Most quantitative comparisons are against IE-AE/raw class-pose outputs, while closely relevant alternatives such as SGM, learned/robust canonicalization variants, data augmentation, equivariant or partially equivariant models, frame averaging, and other symmetry-learning approaches are not fairly compared in the main experiments.

The downstream test-time canonicalization experiment is not convincing enough. The setting is constructed so that canonicalizing synthetic rotations should help a classifier trained on unrotated data, but the comparison to IE-AE is weak and the method is not compared against simpler alternatives such as supervised/unsupervised pose estimators, augmentation-based robustness, or equivariant backbones.

The theoretical result relies on strong and partly circular assumptions: access to good invariant neighborhoods, continuity/equivariance of the learned pose map, small non-group noise, uniqueness and stability of Fréchet means, and the existence of a meaningful natural pose. These assumptions are not adequately validated, and in multimodal settings the proposed robust Fréchet variant is heuristic rather than theoretically integrated into the main proposition.

There are technical inconsistencies and unclear details. For example, the paper alternates between inverse and non-inverse centering conventions in places, uses Fréchet mean language while the SO(3) implementation appears to use matrix-Fisher mode estimation, and some references to tables/figures are confusing or mismatched.

The unsupervised framing is overstated. Although labels may not be used directly by the method, the benchmark construction, ground-truth symmetry definitions, and evaluation all rely on known class- or molecule-level assignments, making the claimed discovery setting less compelling.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper says code will be released or hidden for double blind review, but many important implementation choices, hyperparameter searches, exact model selection criteria, and statistical variability across seeds are not sufficiently reported in the main paper.

The results do not establish robustness. The method depends strongly on the quality of the learned invariant space and kNN neighborhoods; failure modes for mixed classes, object-background scenes, ambiguous symmetries, multimodal pose distributions, and real-world partial symmetries are largely left unexplored.

strengths: The paper identifies a clear and important failure mode of class-pose decomposition methods: learned canonical poses are arbitrary, which makes recovered pose distributions hard to compare and can induce distribution shift for downstream models.

The proposed RECON correction is simple, architecture-agnostic in principle, and well motivated geometrically: estimating a class-level Fréchet/Tukey-Fréchet center and right-normalizing relative poses is an elegant way to obtain data-aligned canonical orientations.

The paper provides a useful theoretical account, including a consistency-style argument for recovering centered symmetry distributions under explicit assumptions, plus a density-invariance result for the OOD scoring formulation.

The empirical scope is broader than much prior work in this area, covering SO(2) image benchmarks and an SO(3) molecular setting, with applications to symmetry recovery, OOD pose detection, and test-time canonicalization.

The results are promising and practically interesting: RECON substantially improves interpretability of recovered distributions, OOD AUC over uncentered IE-AE variants, and test-time accuracy on rotated MNIST/FashionMNIST without retraining the downstream classifier.
weaknesses: The evaluation is still largely based on controlled synthetic pose augmentations. Even the GEOM-QM9 experiment assigns one of only three artificial matrix-Fisher rotation distributions after alignment, so the claim of discovering real-world instance-specific symmetries is stronger than what is directly demonstrated.

Baselines are somewhat limited. The main quantitative comparisons are against IE-AE-style uncentered canonicalization; closer alternatives such as SGM, learned canonicalization/frame averaging variants, supervised or augmentation-based invariance methods, and retraining-based baselines are not consistently evaluated quantitatively.

The method depends heavily on a good class-pose backbone and on nearest-neighbor neighborhoods in the invariant latent space. When the invariant embedding is imperfect, classes overlap, or object-level symmetries are embedded in cluttered scenes, the approach may fail; this is acknowledged but not empirically stress-tested.

The theoretical result relies on strong assumptions, including known group G, continuity and equivariance of the pose estimator, compactness, small non-group residuals, well-behaved Fréchet means, and good recovery of equivalence classes. These assumptions are not fully validated in the more complex experiments.

The 3D results are encouraging but not wholly convincing: performance is summarized through MSE to synthetic matrix-Fisher parameters and qualitative examples, with limited analysis of failure cases and only modest downstream canonicalization gain on GEOM-QM9.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the paper states code will be made available upon publication, while the method involves substantial engineering, long training times, hyperparameter tuning, and several implementation choices that would be hard to reproduce from the manuscript alone.

strengths: The paper tackles a meaningful problem: recovering instance-specific symmetry distributions and correcting the arbitrary canonical orientations produced by class-pose decomposition methods.

The proposed RECON procedure is simple and appealing: estimate the offset of relative poses via a Fréchet/Tukey-Fréchet mean and right-translate the observed pose distribution to obtain a data-aligned canonical orientation.
The work provides a useful theoretical framing with a convergence proposition, plus a practical algorithm and extensions for learned inference-time predictors.

The empirical scope is stronger than many symmetry-learning papers: experiments cover SO(2) image data and SO(3) molecular conformations, with applications to symmetry recovery, OOD pose detection, and test-time canonicalization.

The test-time canonicalization use case is compelling, especially because it can improve frozen non-equivariant backbones without retraining the downstream predictor; the FashionMNIST and GEOM results suggest practical value beyond visual canonicalization.

The paper is generally well written, clearly positioned against class-pose methods, SGM, partial equivariance methods, and canonicalization approaches, and includes substantial implementation details in the appendix.
weaknesses: The strongest empirical settings are still largely synthetic or semi-synthetic: MNIST/FashionMNIST rotations are artificially imposed, and GEOM pose distributions are generated by applying sampled SO(3) rotations. This limits evidence that RECON discovers naturally occurring symmetries in uncontrolled real data.

The method depends heavily on the quality and assumptions of a class-pose decomposition backbone. If the IE-AE pose estimator, invariant space, or nearest-neighbor class approximation is poor, RECON has limited recourse; this dependency is acknowledged but not stress-tested enough.

Baselines for symmetry distribution recovery are incomplete. SGM is discussed as closely related and visually compared, but there is no strong quantitative comparison against SGM or other instance-level distribution estimators on the central task of recovering pose distributions.

The theoretical result relies on strong assumptions, including continuity/compactness, approximate noise-free class generation, uniqueness and stability of Fréchet means, right-invariant metric behavior, and effectively equivariant pose estimates. The paper does not fully characterize failure modes when these assumptions break, especially for multimodal or broad distributions.

The downstream gains are mixed. In GEOM-QM9, RECON improves the frozen GCN only modestly from 52.40% to 55.92%, far below an SE(3)-equivariant SEGNN at 98.55%, so the practical impact in challenging 3D settings is not yet fully convincing.

The claim of plug-and-play inference-time invariance could be interpreted too strongly: while the downstream classifier is frozen, RECON still requires training an IE-AE and learned mappings on the relevant input domain, which is nontrivial and computationally expensive for GEOM.

Ablations are somewhat limited for key design choices such as k-neighbor class construction, Fréchet versus Tukey-Fréchet centering in realistic multimodal cases, robustness to class mixing in latent space, and sensitivity to backbone quality.
Reproducibility is weakened by the missing or incomplete code link in the main text and by some reported results with limited variance information, especially for large-scale GEOM experiments.

strengths: The paper is generally well written and addresses a meaningful problem: recovering instance-specific pose distributions and correcting arbitrary canonical orientations in class-pose decompositions.
The proposed normalization is simple, architecture-agnostic in principle, and practically useful when a class-pose backbone provides reliable invariant embeddings and pose estimates.

The paper includes both SO(2) image experiments and an SO(3) molecular-graph experiment, plus appendices with implementation details, runtime discussion, and analysis of nearest-neighbor class construction.
The downstream applications, especially OOD pose scoring and test-time canonicalization, are intuitive and help clarify why centered pose distributions could be useful.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is quite limited: estimating an offset by a Frechet/circular mean and right-translating pose samples is a natural centering operation. The main proposition largely formalizes this under strong assumptions rather than establishing a surprising or broadly powerful result.

The theoretical guarantee depends on assumptions that are close to the desired conclusion: reliable equivariant pose estimates, compactness/continuity, small non-group noise, a unique and stable Frechet mean, and access to correct equivalence classes. The paper does not convincingly address failure modes when these assumptions break.

The empirical setting is substantially synthetic. MNIST/FashionMNIST rotations are label-designed, and the GEOM-QM9 SO(3) distributions are artificially imposed matrix-Fisher rotations. This weakens claims about discovering real-world intrinsic symmetries.

The comparison set is incomplete for the symmetry-discovery claim. The paper mostly compares against uncentered IE-AE behavior and provides limited quantitative comparison to the most relevant instance-level or distributional symmetry-learning methods such as SGM-style models, VP G-CNNs, Implicit-PDF-like orientation estimators, or strong self-supervised feature baselines.

The downstream canonicalization evaluation has methodological concerns. EquiAdapt hyperparameters appear selected by best test accuracy, and the paper compares an unsupervised canonicalizer trained separately for many hours against baselines under somewhat different supervision/training assumptions. The 'no retraining' framing is also potentially misleading because RECON still requires training an IE-AE and prediction heads.

The GEOM results are not very compelling for downstream utility: RECON improves GCN accuracy from 52.40% to only 55.92%, far below the 98.55% SE(3)-equivariant model. This makes the claimed practical impact in 3D modest.

The method relies critically on nearest-neighbor neighborhoods in the learned invariant space. The appendix shows nontrivial neighbor confusion on FashionMNIST, and the approach may not scale or remain reliable in natural images, multi-object scenes, or settings without clear latent class separation.

Reproducibility is not fully convincing from the manuscript text: the code availability line is incomplete, many results are summarized visually without enough numeric detail, and some experiments report limited variance or only a fixed seed, especially in the molecular setting.
Overall, the paper has a coherent idea and some useful demonstrations, but the novelty, evidence, and evaluation rigor are insufficient for a top-tier AI conference acceptance threshold.

strengths: Clear and meaningful problem formulation: the paper identifies an important issue in class-pose methods, namely arbitrary canonical orientations, and proposes a simple geometric correction that makes recovered pose distributions more interpretable and comparable across instances/classes.

The method is elegant and broadly applicable in principle: estimating a Fréchet/Tukey-Fréchet center of relative poses and right-normalizing by it is architecture-agnostic for any backbone that exposes invariant features and relative group pose.

The empirical scope is stronger than typical work in this area, covering SO(2) image benchmarks and a substantially larger SO(3) molecular conformer setting, with both symmetry recovery and downstream uses.

The downstream applications are compelling: OOD pose detection improves over the uncentered IE-AE baseline, and test-time canonicalization improves frozen classifier accuracy without retraining the downstream backbone.

The paper is generally well positioned against related work on class-pose decompositions, symmetry discovery, partial equivariance, and canonicalization, and the appendices include useful details on neighborhood quality, runtime, and implementation.
weaknesses: The core technical idea is relatively simple, and the novelty depends heavily on the framing and applications rather than a fundamentally new learning mechanism. The theoretical result is mostly a consistency argument under strong assumptions inherited from the class-pose backbone and the latent-neighborhood construction.

The evaluation relies on constructed pose distributions with known synthetic augmentations. This is reasonable for controlled validation, but it leaves open how well RECON discovers naturally occurring, unengineered instance-specific symmetries in real data.

The method depends critically on the quality of the underlying class-pose decomposition and the invariant latent kNN neighborhoods. The paper analyzes this to some extent, but failure modes with latent class overlap, object-centric scenes, multiple objects, or background transformations remain significant.

Some comparisons and claims feel overstated. For example, EquiAdapt and equivariant architectures are not always directly comparable in supervision/training setup, and the GEOM-QM9 canonicalization gain over the frozen baseline is modest despite the large system complexity.

The theory is not fully aligned with practice: the main proof uses the standard Fréchet mean and favorable uniqueness/convexity assumptions, while the robust Tukey-Fréchet variant is introduced heuristically for multimodal cases and is not covered by the same guarantee.

Reproducibility has gaps in the manuscript text: the claimed public code link appears incomplete, and some experimental selection details, such as hyperparameter choice by best test accuracy for baselines, weaken confidence in fair model selection.
